newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan 97/98 wheat production seen at 18 mln T.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan 97/98 wheat production seen at 18 mln T.

text.p: Pakistan is expected to grow 18 million tonnes of wheat in 1997/98 (July-June), up from 16.4 million tonnes in 1996/97 and 16.9 million the previous year, a grain researcher said on Monday.

"I am sure wheat production would be 18 million tonnes, provided the climatic conditions are okay," Abdul Majid, coordinator of the wheat research programme at the state-owned Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, told Reuters.
He said production would rise because yields would improve after the government increased the support price of wheat in April. Leaf rust and yellow rust were not an imminent threat.

"Major wheat-growing areas are not threatened," he said, referring to yellow rust disease, which hit 30 percent of the harvest in 1994/95. "The crop appears to be safe next year, though one cannot say anything with certainty."
Majid said leaf rust fungus usually hits southern Pakistan and yellow rust affects the north, but neither got a chance to spread in last year's drought-like conditions.

Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, India and Nepal are all prone to the fungus, which mutates in three to five years to attack even those varieties previously resistant to the disease. Once it attacks a crop, it shrivels the grain.

Majid said Pakistan had tremendous potential to increase yields from an average of 20 tonnes per acre to more than 40 tonnes per acre if farmers had access to more fertiliser, better seed and improved irrigation facilities.

He said Pakistan now grows wheat on 8.2 million hectares (20.26 million acres), with an average production of 16 to 18 million tonnes a year. The same quantity could be grown on only 2.7 million hectares (6.6 million acres) given the right combination of fertiliser, seed and irrigation.
He said yields would rise if more farmers used certified seeds. Only 10 percent of seeds now used in Pakistan are certified and the rest procured by farmers on their own.
Majid said India enjoyed yields twice as high as Pakistan's because of these factors and Pakistan needed to emulate its neighbour if it was to overcome a chronic wheat shortage.
Pakistan consumes about 19 million tonnes a year, with demand growing by at least three percent annually.
Officials say the government plans to import 4 million tonnes of wheat in 1997/98, double the quantity imported in 1995/96. Majid said this trend must be reversed.
